summary:
Kuwait's Penal Code Article 198 was amended in 2007 by Article 199 bis, which criminalised an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars, about US$3,500. The amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. Human Rights Watch found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised.

In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down the provision as unconstitutional, after an individual who had been targeted by police challenged it. The ruling removed the criminal exposure the article created; it did not end the dress-code policing that preceded and outlasted it. Human Rights Watch called on parliament to repeal the law outright rather than leave it to judicial invalidation. A Library of Congress entry records the same Constitutional Court ruling against Article 198.

Discrimination by officials against transgender people persisted after the 2022 ruling, according to a 2023 assessment one year on. Social and employment discrimination continued, and the ruling was not treated as a step toward recognition of transgender rights. In 2017 Instagram personality King Luxy was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and held for two weeks before release.

Penal Code Article 193 still punishes consensual sexual relations between men by up to seven years, and adultery by up to five years, as recorded in Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 covering events of 2023. Public morality laws are strictly enforced, with prosecutions of LGBTQ people documented. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, or read as such under birth-sex status, faces this exposure regardless of the 2022 Article 198 ruling.

Gender segregation and enforced dress codes make transgender people especially vulnerable across the region, per a 2016 overview essay; the film 'The Danish Girl' was banned by censors in Kuwait. In August 2023 Kuwait banned the film 'Barbie', citing promotion of homosexuality. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information, per the 2023 US State Department country report, and no candidate ran for National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation.

In September 2013 it was announced that Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of 'testing' to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. No implemented entry-screening regime is documented in this record.

Foreign nationals found to be infected with HIV are deported, whereas Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient medical care through a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence remained under 0.1 percent through 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 accounting for 47 percent of those with HIV; the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV in 1992.

No known association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or organise educational and social events. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply; in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops.
tangentialFactors:
A 2018 Human Rights Watch regional study of LGBT activism across 22 Middle East and North Africa jurisdictions, based on interviews with 34 activists, found that six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism. Kuwait was among the jurisdictions covered.

The Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute's July 2024 analysis sets out steps still needed after the abolition of the 'imitating' provision, indicating that decriminalisation in 2022 did not by itself deliver legal recognition or protection.
localsOnly:
Transgender Kuwaitis cannot change their legal documents, per Human Rights Watch's 2008 reporting, and this record does not document any later change to that rule. Social and employment discrimination against transgender people persisted as of February 2023, a year after the Constitutional Court ruling.

Kuwaiti citizens with HIV are entitled to outpatient medical care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital, while foreign nationals found to be infected are deported. The National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV in 1992. No youth-specific or minor-specific care access provisions are documented.

No registered LGBTQ rights association exists. A 2007 application to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form one received no formal reply, and organisers announced in July 2019 they would reapply following a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols in shops.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 Constitutional Court ruling has been followed by legislative repeal of Article 199 bis is unresolved in this record: Human Rights Watch urged parliament to repeal the provision, but no source here confirms repeal, and a 2023 assessment states discrimination by officials persists.

The scale of post-2022 dress-code policing is not sourced. The record documents the ruling and continuing discrimination but provides no figures on enforcement encounters after February 2022.

The 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council 'testing' proposal for detecting homosexuality at entry is documented only as a proposal that officials later disavowed; whether any such screening operates at Kuwaiti ports of entry is not sourced.

Trans-specific violence rates against a general homicide baseline are not present in this inventory, so no comparative risk figure can be stated.
